title: Exclusive: ‘There was no monitoring.’ Sources say FAA had little oversight of work that led to nationwide ground stop
content: On the morning of last week’s historic nationwide ground stop , an FAA technician escorted a private contractor from L3Harris into a remote radio communications site for air traffic control centers in south Arkansas, to replace a decades-old router. The FAA technician believed his role ended when the contractor entered the facility. He went about his own work without knowing exactly what the L3Harris engineer was doing, according to two sources familiar with what happened in the room, and the union that represents FAA technicians. Not long after it was replaced, that new router triggered a cascade of communications problems, flooding the FAA’s aging network with data and leading the FAA to take the rare step later that day of issuing a full nationwide ground stop. About 3,500 planes were in the air when departures were halted for more than four hours while the agency worked to figure out the problem. The details of how that router was installed and who was overseeing that work is now in dispute and emerging as a key point of tension in unraveling what exactly went wrong that day. FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford has defended the FAA’s modernization process and insisted that the L3Harris engineer performing the upgrade “was monitored by an FAA technician” and that a risk assessment was done beforehand. But sources who spoke to CNN dispute this characterization. The technician “was only there to unlock the door,” one of them said. “There was no monitoring,” another source said. That kind of hands-off arrangement, sources say, is a recent development and represents a stark change from how this kind of maintenance work was handled by previous administrations, when the FAA typically exercised far more oversight of contractors’ work. But in an effort to speed up and streamline the modernization of the nation’s air traffic control system with $12.5 billion from President Donald Trump’s “big beautiful bill,” the administration diminished FAA oversight of this kind of work, the sources said. In a memo dated March 2025, the FAA laid out some key changes to how maintenance and upgrades would be carried out, noting: “It is critical to approve maintenance performed by the Telecommunication Vendors without delay.” Under the policy change, the FAA shifted from receiving maintenance “requests” from its private contractors to receiving “notifications” of intended work, noting that “this work will proceed without FAA approval,” according to the memo. The memo does note that an FAA liaison will evaluate the “purpose, severity, criticality and impact” of the work, but the sources told CNN there are only a handful of liaisons nationwide processing thousands of notifications. “So what level of oversight are they really doing?” one of the sources said. As a result, the L3Harris contractor at the center of Friday’s outage showed up with just a few days’ notice and conducted the work without any meaningful oversight from the agency, according to the sources and the union. The March 2025 memo “laid the groundwork for what happened last Friday,” the source said. “They’re not requesting to go out anymore. They’re just notifying and going and then they’re doing the work,” the source said. “And that circumvents the operational risk management aspect where the technician before who works for the government could say, no, no. You can’t do that right now.” Elizabeth Doherty, a spokeswoman for the Professional Aviation Safety Specialists union that represents FAA technicians, told CNN the technician’s “orders were to simply let the contractor in the building,” that he “had no direction to help or assist in any way,” and that “no PASS-represented employee was asked to conduct a risk assessment on this particular upgrade.” CNN asked the FAA about the discrepancy over whether an FAA technician was or was not providing real time oversight of the work. “There is a lot of information that we’re trying to track down. So things have been changing,” FAA spokeswoman Hannah Walden told CNN by phone. “It could have been a misunderstanding or whatever. So I’m not saying one way or the other right now. I just am saying we’re trying to provide information as we get it.” In addressing the changes laid out in the 2025 memo, Walden denied oversight has been reduced, saying the policy change “does not change oversight at all. It changes the priority of the work that needs to be done.” The episode underscores the complications that can arise over a communications system that is operated by the federal government yet is owned by a private company, in this case L3Harris, whose telecom network serves as the communications backbone for the nation’s airspace. It also comes as Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy is asking Congress to approve another $50 billion to upgrade the nation’s air traffic control system even as lawmakers question how the billions allocated last year were spent. L3Harris declined to provide any details in response to CNN’s questions. In a statement to CNN, the company said it is “supporting the FAA in its investigation to understand the conditions that led to the Nov. 13 ground stop of our nation’s air travel.” The policy change laid out in the March 2025 memo didn’t come out of nowhere. The sources familiar with what happened before the ground stop said a chronic, yearslong shortage of FAA technicians as well as the Trump administration’s push for speed helped propel it forward. The result, they believe, was less oversight of the contractor on Friday and a much slower recovery, as the FAA struggled to pinpoint the source of the problem. L3Harris notified the FAA on November 9 that it planned to carry out maintenance, replacing a router, at a remote FAA facility in El Dorado, Arkansas, with work set to begin at 9 a.m. on Friday, November 13, one of the sources said. Four days after the notice, the L3Harris worker arrived. Even the time of day the work was scheduled raised eyebrows, given it was at a time of heavy air traffic. The sources say FAA technicians were not consulted about the best time to carry out this work at this facility. By that Friday afternoon, the new router was connected and the L3Harris contractor had left the site with no idea of the chaos that was beginning to unfold, the source said. Hours later, FAA technicians got a call telling them to return to the site to escort the L3Harris engineer back into the facility. The agency scrambled to find the closest available staff to let him in. Hours had passed between the time the engineer had left and the time he returned to retrieve the router, the source said. A former FAA technician told CNN that, for agency technicians, checking in with air traffic controllers before leaving a site is standard practice. It’s not clear if the L3Harris engineer took this step. “As a technician, anytime when I was out there … and I did anything, anything at all to the equipment before I left, I would call up the TRACON or the center or the tower, whatever controllers that had the services that I was providing on that equipment. And I would say, ‘I’m getting ready to leave. Everything look good? Everything okay? You got everything?’ They’d be like, ‘yep,’” the former technician said. “It’s just a practice that you do.” In the immediate aftermath of the ground stop, Duffy was sharply critical of L3Harris, making a point of calling them out in his public remarks. “We need L3Harris or whoever provided that router to us to do a better job,” Duffy said during his Saturday press conference. “Many of our contractors, many or our partners, they take our money and they provide really poor service to us. Full stop.” Yet by Tuesday, Bedford sounded a different tone toward L3Harris. At a news conference, Bedford described the L3Harris contractor who replaced the router as a “highly trained certified engineer, former Air Force veteran, I’m told a generally competent guy doing the work that he has done dozens and dozens of times before.” Asked what oversight the FAA provides when contractors work at FAA facilities, Bedford also said, “There is a comprehensive risk management process with every installation. And that installation happens whether it’s with a contractor or with an FAA employee.” Days earlier, Duffy had defended the timing of the work, pointing out that it was at a remote location. He said he didn’t expect the kind of impact seen last Friday at “smaller locations.”

The FAA's lack of oversight and the subsequent nationwide ground stop highlight the importance of proper monitoring and risk assessment in critical infrastructure management.

title: How important are Nvidia and Jensen Huang to the US economy?
content:
Nvidia and its co-founder Jensen Huang have been at the centre of the artificial intelligence (AI) spending boom.
No company or chief executive has arguably been more consequential to the development of AI in recent years, with the US microchip manufacturer under Huang positioning itself as a critical cog in the development of the world-changing technology.
That partnership has now ended following Huang's resignation over revelations of extramarital affairs, one of which is alleged to have been with a Chinese spy.
The company has been rocked by the scandal, with hundreds of billions of dollars wiped off its stock market value and questions swirling about the extent of the impact of Huang's departure.
While Nvidia is not as much of a household name as other Big Tech players such as Apple, Amazon and Microsoft, the company has been just as integral to the booming US stock market of recent years.
The billions of dollars being funnelled into AI and the construction of data centres has bolstered the American economy, with Nvidia being one of the biggest spenders.
Originally focusing on chips which process graphics for computer games, it pivoted to making the chips used in AI systems and now dominates the market.
It is now one the most valuable firms, worth $3.8 trillion (£2.9 trillion), and on Tuesday said its rapid growth is poised to continue as the firm's quarterly sales doubled from a year earlier.
But there's now an air of uncertainty over Nvidia's future direction. Huang played a major role in the company, leading its shift towards AI, and maintained a firm grip on the company, with up to 200 people directly reporting to him.
Dan Coatsworth, head of markets at investment firm AJ Bell, says because Huang was also a key figure in "flying the flag" to drum up enthusiasm and investment for the wider AI industry, his departure posed a "real risk" that Nvidia could now decide to change its current strategy and rein in spending.
Such a move could spell a wider slowdown in AI investment, which would have an economic impact. How big? That's "unknown", Coatsworth says.
"If they decide to go with the much more cautious route... there could be a knock-on effect in that you have got various companies in the AI infrastructure space suddenly finding they don't have a key source of finance," he says.
Kunjan Sobhani, senior technology industry analyst at Bloomberg Intelligence, expects the impact of Huang leaving to be "limited" for now as Nvidia has strong commitments and a deep order book. But he said this picture could change in the long run.
That is because Nvidia, on its journey to the top of the AI industry, has created a spider's web of deals through what is known as "circular financing".
Not only does it sell microchips to its customers, which include the likes of Meta, SpaceX and OpenAI, it has also provided funds for them and other firms in the supply chain by either handing out loans or investing in them directly.
The practice has prompted concerns among some investors, who worry what might happen if Nvidia were to turn off the spending taps. If investment dried up, would other firms in the supply chain cut spending or jobs themselves? Would that spread to the wider US economy?
That risk is perhaps why tech bosses including Elon Musk and Tim Sweeney, the CEO of Fortnite maker Epic Games, have called for Huang's reinstatement.
Musk claimed that "critical deals" involving Nvidia's technology would be lost following Huang's resignation, which has also prompted a campaign by shareholders and supporters to "Bring Jensen Back".
Huang himself has said he is open to a return, just days after resigning .
Coatsworth says he has never seen circular financing used at this scale before, but admits there are competitive rivals around, which could insulate the wider AI industry from any potential slowdown at the firm.

final_quality.reason: The article provides a clear reason for readers to care, reporting on the potential impact of Jensen Huang's departure on the US economy and the wider AI industry, which could have significant economic implications.

title: Crimean Bridge attacked again, Russian official says
content:
The Crimean Bridge has been attacked by Ukraine for the third time this week, a Russian official has said.
The Moscow-installed head of Crimea, Sergei Aksyonov, confirmed that traffic was temporarily suspended following another strike on the bridge connecting Russia to occupied Crimea.
The critical bridge had already been hit twice earlier in the week resulting in severe damage and part of the bridge collapsing into the water.
The important infrastructure has long been targeted by Ukraine because of its significance as a logistical and symbolic asset to Moscow's war effort.
It comes as Russian President Vladimir Putin meets US President Donald Trump and China's President Xi Jinping on Thursday for landmark talks in China .
Aksyonov confirmed the strike on the bridge in the early hours of Thursday via Telegram, adding that assessment of the damage was under way.
Meanwhile, Ukrainian sources have continued to issue air raid alert warnings overnight for districts just outside of the capital Kyiv.
At least three people were killed in a Russian drone attack on Odesa on Wednesday, according to the regional state administration. Officials described the attack as "brutal and deliberate... directly targeting people and their lives".
President Volodymyr Zelensky has called the initial strikes on the Crimean Bridge as an "unprecedented operation" weeks in the making.
Ukraine used drones and missiles against it on 17 November which brought down a key section of the road.
That section of the double-arched, 12-mile bridge now lies on the seabed, brought down by an arsenal of Ukrainian long-range weaponry in a seven-stage operation culminating in a dramatic collapse.
In response, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov has said the bridge "will be rebuilt, and it will be even better than before".
While Ukrainian forces have struggled to close the bridge for good, recent attempts have brought them closer to destroying the bridge's crucial road and rail route for Russian soldiers heading towards the front line.
Russian forces have also targeted key bridge crossings over the Dnipro River in Kyiv in recent days.
Russian strikes hit the Pivnichnyi (Northern) and Pivdennyi (Southern) bridges causing traffic closures, partial damage to the metro system and some power and water outages.

final_quality.reason: The article reports a significant development in the Russia-Ukraine conflict, providing new information on the repeated attacks on the Crimean Bridge, a critical infrastructure in the region. The article also provides context and quotes from officials on both sides, making it a substantive and important story in the category of international relations.
